title: Learning Discriminative and Generalizable Anomaly Detector for Dynamic Graph with Limited Supervision
claim: Existing scoring yields overlapping, compressed score distributions with ambiguous boundaries; ours separates classes with an explicit, discriminative margin.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right with blue arrow, paired score histograms and thresholds
description: Two side-by-side schematic histogram panels joined by a large blue arrow pointing from (a) to (b). Both have an x-axis labeled Anomaly Score and a legend (red Anomaly, green Normal). In (a), the green normal and red anomaly distributions overlap and are squeezed into a narrow low range near 0.1. Two grey dashed lines mark an 'Ambiguous boundary', and an orange dashed threshold sits far away at 0.5. Annotations read 'AUROC ~ 1.0, F1 score = 0', and red 'Poor discriminability' text has arrows to the tick marks. In (b), the two histograms are cleanly separated. Grey dashed lines at 0.4 and 0.5 mark an 'Explicit boundary', the orange threshold falls on the anomaly distribution, and the annotations read 'AUROC = 1.0, F1 score ~ 0.5'. Green 'Strong discriminability' text sits under the axis. The eye goes first to the overlapping red and green blobs in (a), then follows the arrow to the separated blobs in (b).
caption: Conceptual illustration. (a) Unsupervised methods often yield ambiguous decision boundaries, with anomaly scores collapse into a narrow range. (b) The objective of our framework.
abstract: Dynamic graph anomaly detection is critical for many real-world applications but remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled anomalies. Existing methods are either unsupervised or semi-supervised: unsupervised methods avoid the need for labeled anomalies but often produce ambiguous boundary, whereas semi-supervised methods can overfit to the limited labeled anomalies and generalize poorly to unseen anomalies. To address this gap, we consider a largely underexplored problem: learning a discriminative boundary from normal/unlabeled data, while leveraging limited labeled anomalies \textbf{when available} without sacrificing generalization to unseen anomalies. In this paper, we propose an effective, generalizable, and model-agnostic framework with three main components: (i) residual representation encoding that capture deviations between current interactions and their historical context, providing anomaly-relevant signals; (ii) a restriction loss that constrain the normal representations within an interval bounded by two co-centered hyperspheres, ensuring consistent scales while keeping anomalies separable; (iii) a bi-boundary optimization strategy that learns a discriminative and robust boundary using the log-likelihood distribution modeled by a normalizing flow. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our framework across diverse evaluation settings.
